name: Joules-per-Compute (JPCUB) Benchmark
description: Current joules-per-compute (JPCUB) benchmarks normalize energy consumption per physical gate, conflating logical operations with error-correction overhead. This obscures trade-offs between qubit connectivity, gate fidelity, and fault-tolerant design, hindering equitable comparisons of quantum processors. We propose a revised JPCUB metric that normalizes energy use per logical-qubit operation, isolating logical computation from error-correction infrastructure. The protocol involves executing standardized logical circuits (e.g., Clifford operations) on surface-code qubits, measuring total energy, and decomposing it into logical gate costs and error-correction overhead. By standardizing benchmark circuits and energy measurement techniques, this approach enables reproducible evaluations of quantum architectures. Simulations suggest [to verify] a 2–5× reduction in JPCUB for fault-tolerant systems compared to uncorrected benchmarks, highlighting the interplay between logical efficiency and error-correction demands. ## 1. Introduction Quantum computing architectures face escalating energy demands as they scale, necessitating rigorous metrics to evaluate efficiency. The existing JPCUB benchmark, which quantifies energy per physical gate [arXiv:2006.07065], fails to distinguish between the energy required for logical operations and that consumed by error correction.
